parameters.query:
WITH due AS (
  SELECT id
  FROM topics
  WHERE enabled
    AND next_run_at <= now()
  ORDER BY next_run_at
  LIMIT __ENVVAR:AR_DISPATCH_BATCH_CAP__
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
-- Claim and reschedule are one statement on purpose. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED holds a
-- claimed row for exactly as long as the transaction that took it, so a claim
-- committed before next_run_at moves leaves the row unlocked and still due, which
-- invites the following tick to run it again. Lifting this UPDATE out into a second
-- node or a second statement is that mistake, and it reads as tidying. Run over one
-- set of due rows twice, the folded form takes them on the first pass and nothing on
-- the second. A claim that only SELECTed hands back the same ids both times.

-- LEAST and GREATEST ignore a NULL argument, so a bound the row does not carry is
-- skipped rather than stood in with COALESCE, which would cap a floored interval back
-- to the proposal and leave the floor doing nothing. clampIntervalSeconds in
-- src/lib/schedule.ts is this same rule as TypeScript, and argues both in full.
UPDATE topics AS t
SET next_run_at = now() + make_interval(secs => LEAST(
  t.max_interval_seconds,
  GREATEST(t.min_interval_seconds, t.interval_seconds)
))
FROM due
WHERE t.id = due.id
-- Five columns because this projection is the shape the merged claim stream carries:
-- every branch answers in it, so the nodes past the merge read one item kind rather
-- than one per table. unit_kind is a literal because nothing in a claimed row says
-- which table it came from, and once the branches merge that is the only thing left
-- to route on. RETURNING on an UPDATE reads the row as written, so next_run_at is
-- the time this pass set rather than the one that made the row due.
RETURNING
  t.id,
  t.domain_id,
  'topic'::text AS unit_kind,
  t.name,
  t.next_run_at

WITH due AS (
  SELECT id
  FROM export_subscriptions
  WHERE enabled
    AND next_run_at <= now()
  ORDER BY next_run_at
  LIMIT __ENVVAR:AR_DISPATCH_BATCH_CAP__
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
-- The same statement as Claim Due Topics, against the other schedulable table. One
-- dispatcher reads both the same way, so the two arguments that shape it are written
-- out on that node and are not repeated here: why the claim and the reschedule are
-- folded into one statement, and why the clamp skips a null bound rather than
-- standing it in with COALESCE. What differs is the table, and the projection below.

-- This claim sits beside Claim Due Topics off the Schedule Trigger rather than behind
-- it, and the difference is a multiplication rather than a preference. A Postgres
-- node runs its statement once per INPUT item, mapping the query over every item it
-- was handed, so chained behind that claim this one would run once per claimed topic,
-- each run taking a fresh batch off this table and rescheduling every row in it. Its
-- run count would be settled by what the node in front emitted, a fact about the
-- other table that says nothing about this one. What makes the parallel form run once
-- is the other half: the trigger emits a single item per fire. Neither half implies
-- the other, and without the emit count a branch off the trigger could multiply for
-- the same reason a chained one does.

-- The cap is per claim and not per tick. This LIMIT and the one on Claim Due Topics
-- read one setting, so a tick finding both tables backlogged claims up to twice it,
-- and both claims have already moved next_run_at on every row they took. So the
-- second application of the cap, over the merged stream, is a choice about which
-- claimed rows are RUN and not a re-check of a batch already inside the cap. What it
-- leaves behind was rescheduled without being dispatched, and comes round again a
-- whole interval later. capBatch in src/lib/schedule.ts carries the rest of that
-- argument.
UPDATE export_subscriptions AS s
SET next_run_at = now() + make_interval(secs => LEAST(
  s.max_interval_seconds,
  GREATEST(s.min_interval_seconds, s.interval_seconds)
))
FROM due
WHERE s.id = due.id
-- The five columns Claim Due Topics answers in, plus one of this branch's own.
-- export_subscriptions carries no name, so the label is the format, which is what the
-- row renders. It does not identify the row: a domain may take one format at two
-- destinations, and connector_id is what tells those apart. That column rides on this
-- branch alone, so nothing past the merge may read one off an arbitrary claimed unit.
-- unit_kind is 'export' rather than this table's own singular because it names the
-- dispatch the row asks for, and pairs with AR_EXPORT_WORKFLOW_ID the way 'topic'
-- pairs with AR_TOPIC_WORKFLOW_ID.
RETURNING
  s.id,
  s.domain_id,
  'export'::text AS unit_kind,
  s.format AS name,
  s.next_run_at,
  s.connector_id

nodes.name: Merge Claims
nodes.notes: Append, so what leaves here is the two claim branches concatenated: nothing is dropped, added or rewritten, and a table with nothing due never holds the tick, append needing data from only one input to continue. What it does not pass on is which branch an item came in on, which is what unit_kind stands in for downstream. A tick claiming nothing does not arrive as nothing: a Postgres node whose statement is not a SELECT emits one success item when it returns no rows, so an empty tick reaches here as two items carrying no unit_kind. Dropping them belongs to the Code node, keyed on the absent unit_kind rather than on a branch.

parameters.query:
INSERT INTO runs (domain_id, scheduled_by)
-- One row per CLAIMED UNIT rather than one per tick, and nothing in this statement
-- says so. An executeQuery node maps its query over the items it was handed and runs
-- it once per INPUT item, so the multiplication the two claims are wired in parallel
-- to avoid is exactly the behaviour wanted here. Every item that reaches this node is
-- a unit Plan Dispatch kept, which makes the row count the tick's dispatch count.
-- What holds it that way is the two things this node does not carry: no executeOnce,
-- and a domain read off $json rather than off the whole batch. Either one would turn
-- this back into a single row per tick without touching a clause.

-- The per-unit row is what the two columns above are worth anything for. scheduled_by
-- is NOT NULL because attributing a fired schedule afterwards is the whole of its
-- job, and a tick-level row files every claimed row's schedule under one answer,
-- which is the limit runs.scheduled_by in src/db/schema/runs.ts already records for a
-- pass claiming several due rows at once. domain_id is the other half: topics and
-- export_subscriptions both declare it NOT NULL, so every claimed unit carries a real
-- domain, while a tick spans every domain at once and could only write NULL. On runs
-- that NULL is not an empty slot but a meaning of its own, that the pass was not
-- scoped to a domain, so a tick-level dispatch row would be stored looking exactly
-- like the maintenance and backfill passes that legitimately carry none.

-- Two honest limits. A tick claiming nothing opens no row at all, Plan Dispatch
-- having dropped both empty-result placeholders before anything reaches here, so runs
-- records what the dispatcher dispatched and never whether it ran. That question is
-- answered from the executor's own execution list instead. And a per-unit row makes
-- the attribution as fine as one claim without making the interval literal below any
-- truer: nothing in a claimed row records which of the three modes wrote its
-- next_run_at, all of them writing that one column, which is why
-- src/db/schema/scheduling.ts has the choosing logged on the run rather than read
-- back off it. So interval here names the mode THIS workflow reschedules in, not the
-- mode that set the time this pass fired against.

-- One question this statement leaves open, and it is the table's gap rather than a
-- third limit of the choice above. runs carries no column naming the workflow that
-- opened a row. The column list above is the whole of what this insert supplies, and
-- the six src/db/schema/runs.ts adds to it are a surrogate key, a start, a finish, a
-- status, a tally and a list of failures, none of which says who wrote the row. The
-- question is answerable today all the same, by convention rather than by reading:
-- ar-dispatch is the only workflow that opens one, so every row a workflow opened
-- came out of this statement and the answer belongs to the table instead of to the
-- row.

-- The convention holds exactly as long as its premise does. The roster in
-- workflows/src/README.md delivers ar-ingest, ar-capture and ar-score in phase 5, and
-- the first of them to open a run of its own leaves two workflows sharing one table
-- with nothing in a row to tell their passes apart. What is stored narrows without
-- naming: domain_id says which domain a pass ran for, and several workflows will run
-- for the same domain, while scheduled_by carries the one literal below for every row
-- this workflow opens. counts and errors refuse nothing, so a producer's name dropped
-- into either is one writer's habit rather than a column a reader can query. Closing
-- the gap is a column and a column is a migration this phase does not carry, so it is
-- left here for phase 5, which is the phase that has to choose between the column and
-- a second convention.
VALUES ($1::bigint, 'interval')
RETURNING id AS run_id

nodes.name: Invoke Target Workflow
nodes.notes: Run once for each item is a requirement and not a tuning choice: the once mode resolves ONE workflow id, from the first input item, and sends every claimed unit to it, which would put every export subscription through the topic workflow. The id is read off Plan Dispatch rather than $json because the Postgres node in front replaces an item's json with its own RETURNING projection, leaving a run id and nothing of the claimed unit; pairedItem carries the lineage that far. Waiting for the sub-workflow is the default written out, a run closed by outcome needing one: without it a unit reaches the success output as soon as its sub-execution starts. onError puts a failure on a second output the executor appends here; continuing on the REGULAR output would hand a failed invocation to Close Run Succeeded.

parameters.query:
UPDATE runs
-- Closes the run Open Run opened for this unit, on the output the executor appends
-- when Invoke Target Workflow fails. Every unit reaching that node already has a row
-- here, so this statement finishes one and never writes one: a row exists for what
-- the tick dispatched, and this branch settles how it went.

-- failed rather than partial, because the run's whole work was the one invocation.
-- partial is the member for a pass that produced real work and a real failure at
-- once, and no such split is available here: a unit is dispatched or it is not.

-- status and finished_at are set together because nothing in the schema holds them
-- together. src/db/schema/runs.ts records that a row saying failed with no finish, or
-- carrying a finish while still saying running, is storable, and that only the writer
-- pairs them. This statement is that writer for the rows this workflow opens.

-- The entry is APPENDED and not written over. runs.errors is one entry per failure
-- defaulting to an empty list, and this row's id does not stay inside this workflow:
-- Open Run's projection is the item Invoke Target Workflow forwards to the target, so
-- a target that recorded its own failure against this run before failing has entries
-- here already. Assigning a fresh list would drop them and leave the dispatcher's
-- account of the failure standing as the whole of it.

-- The entry names the target that could not be invoked and the executor's own
-- message. A null target is an answer rather than a missing one: Plan Dispatch passes
-- on a unit whose kind it has no entry for carrying a null where an id belongs, and
-- that unit and one carrying a good id with no workflow behind it fail onto this same
-- branch. The route cannot tell those apart and the stored entry can, a JSON null
-- naming the routing miss where a string names the id that had nothing behind it.

-- Both jsonb parameters are handed over as JSON TEXT rather than as bare values, and
-- that is what makes the statement safe rather than what makes it tidy. A query
-- parameter is split on commas unless it parses as JSON on its own, and an executor's
-- message routinely carries one, so a bare message would arrive as two values and the
-- statement would be refused for a parameter count it never asked for. Stringifying
-- makes every possible answer parse, so each is taken whole. It carries the null too,
-- which reaches jsonb as a null and not as a string spelling one. The run id needs no
-- wrapper for the narrower reason that a number already parses as JSON.
SET
  status = 'failed',
  finished_at = now(),
  errors = errors || jsonb_build_array(jsonb_build_object(
    'node', 'Invoke Target Workflow',
    'target_workflow_id', $2::jsonb,
    'error', $3::jsonb
  ))
WHERE id = $1::bigint

parameters.query:
UPDATE runs
-- Closes the run Open Run opened for this unit, on the output Invoke Target Workflow
-- takes when its invocation returns. Close Run Failed is the same statement on that
-- node's other output, and the two arguments the pair shares are written out there
-- rather than repeated here: why a row always exists for this to finish and never to
-- write, and why status and finished_at have to be set together.

-- ok is what a finished pass with nothing to report carries. RUN_STATUSES in
-- src/db/schema/values.ts holds no member spelled succeeded, and ok rather than
-- partial follows Close Run Failed's reason for failed rather than partial: from this
-- workflow's side the run's whole work was the one invocation, and a unit is either
-- dispatched or it is not.

-- What that reading leaves open is a question about the row rather than about this
-- statement. The run id Open Run returned is the item Invoke Target Workflow forwards
-- to the target, so a target can write entries into this row's errors and still
-- return. This statement does not read that column, so such a run closes ok while
-- carrying the entries that make partial the accurate member, a pairing
-- src/db/schema/runs.ts records as storable and leaves entirely to the writer. This
-- writer takes the invocation's outcome as the whole answer. Nothing reaches the case
-- yet, no target existing until phase 5, which is the phase that has to choose
-- between reading errors here and holding every target to reporting its own status.

-- The run id is read off Open Run rather than off $json, for a different reason than
-- the same read has on the failed branch. Invoke Target Workflow waits for the
-- sub-workflow, so what arrives here is the TARGET's output and neither the claimed
-- unit nor the run row survives the invocation. What does survive is pairedItem, set
-- to the input index on every item forwarded, and that is the whole of what makes
-- $('Open Run').item resolve here.

-- Two honest limits, both of them counts rather than values, and both settled by the
-- target's contract rather than by anything here. The first is that this node runs
-- once per item on the success output, which is not once per dispatched unit: the
-- items are whatever the target returned, so a target answering with three items
-- closes one run three times. The repeats cost nothing past the writes. They agree on
-- the status, and they agree on the finish as well, a node execution sending its
-- whole batch as one query string and Postgres running that as one transaction, which
-- is what fixes now() across it.

-- That same fixing is worth reading the other way, because it says what the column
-- holds. Every run this node closes in a tick carries one finish, and it is the time
-- the dispatcher closed them rather than the time any target stopped working.

-- The second limit is the other end of the count. A target answering with NO items
-- puts nothing on this output at all, so its run is never closed: it keeps the
-- running status Open Run left it at, which src/db/schema/runs.ts records as the
-- member no writer reports and which nothing here can age out, a row whose pass died
-- reading exactly like one still working. Phase 5 writes the first target and is
-- where both limits stop being hypothetical.
SET
  status = 'ok',
  finished_at = now()
WHERE id = $1::bigint

parameters.content:
## Build Stamp

**__ENVVAR:AR_BUILD_TAG__**

The git short commit `scripts/build-workflows.ts` resolved when it wrote this artifact. A stamp that does not match the commit you deployed means the instance is running an older import.

`dev` is a build with no commit to name, and a `-dirty` suffix a tree carrying uncommitted changes. Neither is an older import.
